Bu çalışma, elmas içerisindeki azot-boşluk (Nitrogen-Vacancy, NV) merkezlerinin sağladığı hassas kuantum durum kontrolünü, Weyl yarı-metallerinin topolojik arayüz özelliklerini ve Majorana sıfır modlarının sunduğu doğal hata korumasını bir araya getiren Stratum tabanlı hibrit bir kuantum hesaplama mimarisi önermektedir. Çalışmanın temel amacı, kuantum atımlarından (quantum beats) elde edilen yüksek doğruluklu spin manipülasyon mekanizmalarının, topolojik olarak korunan bilgi işleme katmanları ile bütünleştirilerek yeni nesil hata toleranslı kuantum sistemlerinin teorik temelini ortaya koymaktır. Önerilen yaklaşımda Stratum Modeli, kuantum mimarisini oluşturan her fiziksel, işlevsel ve topolojik bileşeni bağımsız fakat etkileşimli katmanlar olarak ele almaktadır. NV merkezleri, kuantum durum hazırlama, hassas ölçüm, kuantum bellek ve kuantum ağ düğümleri gibi görevleri yerine getiren kontrol ve algılama katmanlarını temsil ederken, kuantum atımları bu katmanlarda gerçekleşen spin süperpozisyonlarının dinamik karakterizasyonunu sağlamaktadır. Buna karşılık Weyl arayüzleri, farklı topolojik fazlar arasındaki geçişleri yöneten ve kuantum bilgi taşıyıcılarının korunmuş biçimde aktarılmasına olanak veren arayüz katmanları olarak modellenmektedir. Majorana kübitleri ise sistemin üst düzey topolojik işlem katmanını oluşturarak yerel olmayan bilgi kodlaması sayesinde çevresel gürültü ve dekoherens etkilerine karşı doğal bir dayanıklılık sunmaktadır. Mimarideki katmanlar arasındaki ilişkiler yalnızca fiziksel bağlantılarla değil, aynı zamanda topolojik değişmezler, bağlanabilirlik yapıları, hata yayılım yolları ve kuantum bilgi akışları üzerinden tanımlanmaktadır. Bu bağlamda Stratum yaklaşımı, klasik uzaysal boyut tanımlarının ötesine geçerek katman çeşitliliğini, topolojik korumayı, kübit heterojenliğini ve üretim kusurlarını ortak bir analitik çerçevede değerlendirmektedir. Ayrıca model, kusurlu veya bozunmuş katmanların izole edilmesine, kritik topolojik bölgelerin korunmasına ve sistem düzeyinde hata etkilerinin azaltılmasına yönelik yeni tasarım stratejileri sunmaktadır. Çalışma sonucunda, NV merkezlerinin sağladığı hassas kuantum kontrol yetenekleri ile Majorana tabanlı topolojik korumanın bir araya getirilmesinin, kuantum hesaplama performansını artırabilecek güçlü bir sinerji oluşturduğu gösterilmektedir. Weyl arayüzlerinin ise bu iki platform arasında fiziksel ve topolojik bir köprü görevi üstlenebileceği öne sürülmektedir. Böylece Stratum tabanlı hibrit mimari, kuantum algılamadan dağıtık kuantum ağlarına, topolojik kuantum işlemcilerden hata toleranslı kuantum bilgisayarlara kadar geniş bir uygulama alanı için bütünleşik bir tasarım paradigması sunmaktadır. Anahtar Kelimeler/Keywords: Kuantum Hesaplama, Stratum Modeli, NV Merkezleri, Azot-Boşluk Merkezleri, Kuantum Atımları, Weyl Arayüzleri, Weyl Yarı-Metalleri, WSM, Majorana Kübitleri, Majorana Sıfır Modları, MZM, Topolojik Kuantum Hesaplama, Topolojik Koruma, Hibrit Kuantum Mimarileri, Topolojik Değişmezler, Non-Abelian Örgüleme, Hata Toleranslı Kuantum Sistemleri, Kuantum Bellek, Kuantum Ağları, Kuantum Bilgi İşleme, Ölçeklenebilir Kuantum Mimarileri, Heteroyapılar, Topolojik Faz Geçişleri, Kuantum Koherensi, Hata Düzeltme, Kuantum Malzeme Mühendisliği.

title: GENERATIVE AI MARKETING AND PURCHASE INTENTION AMONG GENERATION Z: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF BRAND PERCEPTION
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping digital marketing by enabling personalised, scalable, and innovative content, while simultaneously raising concerns regarding authenticity and consumer trust. This study examines how Perceived Authenticity, Perceived Personalization, and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation influence Brand Perception and Purchase Intention among Generation Z consumers, with Brand Perception serving as a mediating mechanism. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using data from 425 Generation Z consumers collected through a structured questionnaire based on five-point Likert-type scales. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson and Spearman correlations, multiple regression, variance inflation factors, HC3 robust standard errors, and bootstrapped mediation analysis based on 5,000 resamples. The findings indicate that Perceived Authenticity (β = .234), Perceived Personalization (β = .160), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .407) significantly and positively influence Brand Perception. Brand Perception significantly predicts Purchase Intention (β = .520). Significant indirect effects were observed for Perceived Authenticity (β = .122), Perceived Personalization (β = .083), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .212) through Brand Perception. The findings demonstrate that consumer responses to GenAI marketing translate into purchase intention substantially through broader brand evaluations. The study highlights the importance of combining AI-enabled innovation and personalization with authenticity and consistent brand positioning.

title: Hierarchical Detection of Encrypted UAV Communication Traffic for Low-Altitude Ground-Side Monitoring
abstract: Ground-side monitors may observe UAV communication alongside ordinary IP traffic, even when application payloads are encrypted or removed during capture. Detection then relies on observable packet metadata: packet length, inter-arrival time, direction, and transport protocol. Changes in platforms, communication patterns, and link conditions can also produce target UAV traffic absent from training. A detector must therefore retain training-unseen UAV communication while rejecting non-UAV background traffic with similar local statistics. We propose a hierarchical detector for IP-based UAV communication. It converts bidirectional packet streams into fixed-length windows, learns multi-scale temporal representations, screens the target UAV support space, and assesses candidate and boundary windows using periodic and morphological descriptors. We evaluate known and training-unseen UAV traffic, mixed non-UAV background traffic, controlled perturbations, and limited external-domain cases. The method provides communication-side evidence for IP-based UAV activity and is intended to complement physical sensing; radio links without an observable IP/transport layer remain outside its scope.

title: Finite-sample certification of coverage regret for budgeted document selection under adaptive stratified auditing
abstract: Selecting a budget-constrained set of documentary fragments, for instance the knowledge base of a retrieval-augmented generation system, raises a statistical question: how much expected query coverage is lost relative to the best feasible selection when the query distribution is unknown? We construct finite-sample, distribution-free upper confidence bounds for this coverage regret that remain valid after data-dependent selection. A pilot stage may select the document set, screen competitors, build comparison networks and learn an annotation policy. Then an independent audit acquires relevance labels with probabilities that are constant within observable strata. The main result is a simultaneous bound for all retained coverage contrasts. The bound is made observable by empirical-Bernstein variance calibration or by a one-stage construction without calibration, and it accounts for estimated stratum proportions. For maximum-type coverage we prove variance contractions for swaps of redundant fragments, give a condition under which multiscale radii improve on a direct union bound, and show that such redundancy cannot be certified from samples alone. A simulation study confirms validity and quantifies the gains from variance calibration and certified redundancy.

title: Visual Tokens on Demand: Visual Budgeting for Scalable and Efficient Multi-Image Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Multimodal large language models have advanced rapidly, but most remain optimized for single-image inputs. Multi-image reasoning is costly because each image adds many visual tokens, increasing encoding and attention demands. Existing techniques that address the above issue, including visual token pruning, token merging, visual token compression, learned resampling, hierarchical compression, retrieval-augmented visual reasoning, and memory-based architectures, have largely been designed for single-image scenarios, where redundancy is primarily spatial and local. Multi-image reasoning introduces additional challenges: redundancy may occur across images, task-relevant evidence may be sparse or distributed, and aggressive per-image compression can remove details needed for comparison, counting, temporal reasoning, retrieval, or evidence grounding. Moreover, existing token-reduction methods are often either (i) training-free but inference-inefficient, typically relying on accessing attention matrices to get token-importance that may be impractical to access with memory-efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention, or (ii) training-dependent, requiring the base MLLM to be retrained or adapted to a new compressed-token paradigm. In this work, we study scalable multi-image reasoning and understanding without retraining the base model and without accessing attention matrices at inference time. To this end, we propose mmVB, a lightweight plug-and-play module that assigns query-conditioned per-image token budgets via cross-image context, adding only 1.6M trainable parameters while reducing visual input tokens by 9x. This reduction yields 5x faster time-to-first-token and 7x fewer prefill FLOPs, while maintaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight multi-image reasoning benchmarks.

title: $\mathsf{EFI}\Leftrightarrow\mathsf{1PRS}$
abstract: A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.

title: LoopREG: Representation Supervision Enables Test-Time Recurrent Depth in Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Reusing Transformer blocks offers a way to increase diffusion-model computation at test time, but naive recurrence can degrade generation beyond its training depth. We introduce LoopREG, a representation-supervised recurrent diffusion Transformer that repeatedly applies a shared block at the state supervised by a pretrained visual encoder. Alignment is applied after the final recurrent visit during training; inference extends the same learned operator to additional visits. On ImageNet 256 x 256, LoopREG reduces SiT-B/2 FID from the local REG baseline's 15.08 to 4.91 at 400K training steps, a 67.41% reduction. Within a checkpoint trained with two visits, one extra inference visit improves FID from 14.71 to 5.34 with unchanged weights. The benefit persists on SiT-L/2 and SiT-XL/2. Controlled interventions show that useful recurrence follows the location of representation supervision, while REPA alignment produces a smaller extrapolation benefit. These results make representation-supervised recurrence a practical route to improving diffusion generation through additional inference depth.

title: Encoding Context into LLM Weights: What Makes It Context?
abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.

title: Text-Only vs. Image-Aware VLM Judges for Manga Translation Evaluation
abstract: In manga translation, visual context outside speech-bubble text, including speaker identities, referents, and scene tone, is depicted in page images, making it natural to refer to images during translation evaluation. However, most conventional manga translation evaluations rely solely on text-only automatic metrics, leaving the impact of image input insufficiently explored. We propose a practical validation framework that employs the same vision-language model (VLM) as both a text-only judge (TOJ) and an image-aware judge (IAJ) to investigate evaluation divergences associated with image-aware evaluation procedures. We use a Japanese-English manga dataset of official translations aligned at the page and speech-bubble levels. First, adding page images to TOJ improved the primary VLM's detection of deliberately injected, visually dependent degradations. Second, we analyzed evaluation divergences between TOJ and IAJ, finding different error counts and error-category distributions. Human verification did not reveal a consistent preference between TOJ and IAJ.

title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

title: Teach Me After You Learn It: Lookahead Self-Distillation for RLVR
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a popular training paradigm for LLMs, providing dense, token-level supervision by aligning a model's own distribution with the distribution induced by privileged information. However, existing OPSD methods derive supervision solely from privileged information of the same instance, leaving inter-instance supervision largely unexplored. We propose Lookahead Self-Distillation (LEAD), which introduces inter-instance distillation by allowing the teacher to first learn from other on-policy rollouts before teaching the student. LEAD constructs lookahead teachers through virtual RL updates on disjoint subsets of on-policy rollouts, and uses each teacher to provide cross-group token-level supervision for the other subset. To reconcile the complementary yet potentially conflicting signals from OPSD and RLVR, we introduce harmonious modulation, which adaptively modulates the GRPO advantage based on the agreement between the two signals. Extensive experiments on scientific reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks show that LEAD achieves the best in-domain average performance across model scales while maintaining out-of-domain generalization comparable to GRPO.

title: zPocket: Better Pocket Finding with Frozen Co-Folding Features
abstract: Identifying protein-ligand binding sites (pockets) is important for understanding protein function and developing drugs. However, no public method has leveraged co-folding models for novel pocket prediction; furthermore, this task lacks a suitable benchmark as existing benchmarks are within the training distribution of co-folding models. We therefore developed PocketWatch,a curated dataset of biologically relevant ligand pockets. The PocketWatch test set consists of unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity to enable evaluation of generalization to novel and challenging pockets. Using this dataset, we develop zPocket, a method that trains pocket-prediction heads on top of frozen features from co-folding models. We show that zPocket heads outperform baseline methods across all stratifications. Our best zPocket model achieves overall per-target AUPRC of 0.745 compared to 0.598 and 0.595 for the strongest baselines, VN-EGNN and UniSite-1D retrained on the PocketWatch split (0.559 and 0.531 when using the published weights); the widely used P2Rank reaches 0.477. We further show that zPocket can be used to outperform baseline methods on top-N+2 recall of predicted pocket centroids through clustering per-residue predictions or using zPocket to rescore centroids proposed by other models. Finally, we explore two applications of zPocket: crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins. Together these results suggest that zPocket heads built on co-folding trunk features can greatly advance ligand binding site prediction.

title: SparPR: Runtime KV-Cache Recovery for Resource-Constrained LLM Inference on Consumer Hardware
abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. SparPR couples three online decisions: Query-Aware key-block selection scores historical blocks against the current query; dynamic budget control estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain; and on-demand local recomputation with cost-aware fallback merges retained blocks into continuous spans and switches between sparse recomputation and full recovery according to a runtime cost comparison. Implemented on FlexGen/FlexLLMGen, SparPR is evaluated on a single consumer laptop (RTX 3070 Ti 8GB, Ryzen 9 6900HX, 16GB RAM). It cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens respectively, with 1.4x-2.7x higher throughput, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the FlexGen baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget, SparPR retains a Needle Accuracy that stays well above StreamingLLM and H2O at every keep ratio, and ablation studies confirm that the three mechanisms act jointly.

title: RLPE: Teaching LLMs to Prompt with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Prompting is a widely used method for adapting general-purpose LLMs to domain-specific tasks. Effective prompts can be tedious to create manually, so prompt writing is increasingly handed to LLMs, with recent work training LLMs to write prompts for other models. These techniques either write prompts without observing how the task model behaves, blind to the failure modes the prompt should address, or must run alongside the task LLM at inference time, adding overhead to every query. Neither reflects how prompt engineering is often practiced. To close this gap, we introduce Reinforcement Learned Prompt Engineering (RLPE), which trains a model to analyze traces of a separate task model and write a prompt targeting the failures it observes. RLPE rewards the trained model strictly on prompt performance, so it learns the prompting strategies that improve the task model. The prompt is generated once and reused across the task, so inference does not require the trained model. Since RLPE needs only query access to the model it prompts, it is also compatible with closed-source models. We apply RLPE to Enigmata, BIG-Bench Extra Hard, and PlanBench. We train a 9B-parameter model that writes better prompts than state-of-the-art frontier models (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-opus-5) and prompt optimizers (GEPA and TextGrad) on 2/3 benchmarks. Although the model is never explicitly trained to iterate on prompts, this capability emerges at a level that matches or beats frontier models. The learned prompting capability also generalizes, with the trained model improving task models 6x larger than the one it trained with, including ones from entirely different model families, and matching claude-opus-5 on a fourth benchmark held out from training.

title: Análisis Exploratorio de Datos con Pandas en Python
abstract: En este laboratorio se realiza un análisis exploratorio de datos utilizando la biblioteca Pandas en Python, con el objetivo de comprender la estructura, características y relaciones de un conjunto de datos. A través de la carga, exploración, limpieza, etc., se aplican técnicas fundamentales que permiten preparar los datos para análisis posteriores y apoyar la toma de decisiones informadas.

title: Reliable model validation under class imbalance: reproducibility code and results
abstract: v1.0.0 – Initial reproducibility release Initial public reproducibility release associated with the study: Practical Guidelines for Permutation-Based Model Validation in Machine Learning under Class Imbalance This release contains: the final nested-validation implementation; AdaBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, and XGBoost workflows; FP and FPs prediction formulations; permutation-testing implementation; 720 derived permutation AUC results; observed-label validation summaries; manuscript-ready figures; reproducibility and computational-environment documentation. Data The raw aero-engine data are not included in this software release. Data are maintained separately and may be made available through a separate Zenodo data record, subject to the applicable redistribution permissions. Computing Large-scale AdaBoost, Random Forest, and XGBoost experiments were run using the University of Leicester ALICE High Performance Computing Facility. LightGBM permutation experiments were completed on a local Apple Silicon workstation. Licence Source code is released under the MIT License.

title: Echoes of Thought: Task Complexity, Inner Speech Analogs, and Prompt Design Shape LLMs’ Response Behavior in the Two-Step Task
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, yet the mechanisms behind their response behavior remain poorly understood. Drawing on insights from cognitive science and the computational framework of model-free and model-based reinforcement learning (RL), we examined conditions under which GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs can exhibit behavioral signatures of model-based RL in the two-step task, a well-established paradigm for studying human learning and decision-making. Across nine simulation studies, we varied the task complexity and prompt design to examine conditions under which previously reported model-based RL signatures could be replicated. We found that GPT-3.5 showed model-based RL signatures in simplified task settings, but that these effects disappeared under de-simplified task versions. Crucially, model-based reasoning signatures could be re-established when incorporating an inner speech-analog prompt, requiring the LLM agent to reflect on previous trials and anticipate consequences of future actions. For the open-weight LLMs tested, we observed diminished signatures of model-based reasoning under both de-simplified and facilitative task conditions. Our fine-grained analyses of behavioral learning dynamics highlight the role of structured reflective and anticipatory linguistic processes in enabling complex response patterns in LLMs and reveal both similarities to and differences from human decision-making patterns.

title: A Comprehensive Survey on LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search
abstract: Large Language Model-guided Evolutionary Search (LLM-ES), exemplified by AlphaEvolve, has recently demonstrated impressive performance in solving goal-driven problems with extremely large and complex search spaces. Unlike conventional LLM approaches based on single-shot or few-shot sampling, LLM-ES introduces population-based evolution to iteratively generate more novel and higher-quality solutions. Compared with traditional Evolutionary Computing algorithms, LLM-ES treats LLMs as semantic variation operators. This design extends the search space from low-dimensional vectors to expressive and language-defined structures such as code and programs. Meanwhile, the rich prior knowledge embedded in LLMs significantly improves the efficiency of evolutionary search in complex solution spaces. As a result, LLM-ES effectively exploits the test-time scaling capability of LLMs and achieves state-of-the-art performance in many open-ended problems. In this survey, we provide a systematic overview of this emerging field. We first formalize the problem setting and the general pipeline of LLM-ES. We then review existing works from several key perspectives, including population design, prompt builder, LLM model selection, evaluation design, and exploration-exploitation control. Finally, we summarize representative applications and discuss open challenges and future research directions.

title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting: Continual Learning for Radar Waveform Classification
abstract: Automated radar waveform recognition classifies the waveform and modulation type of a received signal. As new waveform variants appear over time, a deployed classifier must learn them without retraining from scratch. Catastrophic Forgetting occurs when learning new waveforms overwrites prior knowledge. Continual Learning (CL) methods tackle this challenge, but prior radar studies only evaluate a few methods on narrow benchmarks. Practitioners lack evidence on which method to deploy or which mechanisms are effective. This work presents the first large-scale benchmark of continual learning for radar waveform recognition. Eighteen CL methods are evaluated on a sequential ten-task problem, drawn from four public datasets spanning 54 waveforms, under task- and class-incremental (TIL, CIL) settings and single- and multi-epoch regimes. Methods that retain data from old tasks lead both TIL and CIL settings. Plain replay alone closes 77-88% of the gap between the lower and upper practical limits under TIL, but only 46-55% under CIL. The internal mechanisms of the leading methods are ablated and statistically tested to identify effective mechanisms. Each ablation is paired against its full method over n=6 training seeds, topped up to n=12 when inconclusive, and p-values are Holm-Bonferroni corrected within each method's family. Ablation results show that several mechanisms confer smaller but statistically significant gains. Combining these mechanisms improves the leading F1 score by 3.4-5.5% and 2.7-4.9% under TIL and CIL, respectively, and the combined models exceed every benchmarked method in both settings for all SNRs. These results give researchers of radar waveform classification systems a mechanism-level basis for design.

title: Cheap, Consistent, Calibrated, but Biased? Typed Decision Models as Judges
abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability for each allowed answer instead of generating text, which makes them candidates for cheaply replacing LLM judges that compare two answers. Whether they share the biases of LLM judges is untested. We run the CALM benchmark's bias tests on eight TDMs and seven LLM judges of 2024 and 2026. Every TDM is biased, in three to eight of twelve tests. Emotional tone affects them most, and rewriting the better answer in such a tone lowers the accuracy of a typical TDM from 99% to 42%. TDMs are more biased than 2026 LLM judges. All eight change verdicts when the answers swap places, which the 2026 LLM judges hardly do, and several side with an answer that most people allegedly prefer or that a famous model allegedly wrote. Yet both kinds of judge are tripped up by the same prompts. The TDMs' probabilities show that most tests mainly flip verdicts the TDM was unsure of, and that good calibration does not protect against bias. As TDMs are more consistent and 37 times cheaper than 2026 LLM judges, our results suggest they can be attractive judges if their biases are tested for the task.

title: Searching for What Matters: Open-Ended Discovery of Multiple Hypotheses with Agentic Data Exploration
abstract: Discovering what drives an outcome from data is central to science and often requires deciding what is worth investigating before a specific hypothesis is known. Yet most existing hypothesis generation settings substantially narrow this search by providing a research question, target relationship, or curated context. We introduce open-ended multiple hypothesis discovery, where a system receives only a large tabular dataset and an outcome and must discover multiple data-supported hypotheses without knowing in advance the relevant variables, functional forms, conditions, or number of underlying mechanisms. To study this problem, we introduce a benchmark built from structural causal models grounded in real-world data schemas, containing 351 planted hypotheses across 15 tasks and five domains, with 53--65 variables and 1M--10M rows per task. The causal model is hidden from the discovery method and retained only by the evaluator, allowing proposed hypotheses to be tested through interventions and separating observational discovery from causal validation. We further propose HypAgent, which treats the dataset as an interactive environment and performs iterative search by proposing candidate directions, triaging and refining promising hypotheses, and removing explained signal so that each accepted discovery redirects subsequent search. HypAgent achieves 0.47 precision, 0.51 recall, and 0.49 F1, compared with 0.35 F1 for the strongest baseline. Our analysis shows that many failures occur after a relevant variable has already been surfaced, suggesting that correctly characterizing a mechanism's functional form and conditions, rather than merely identifying relevant variables, remains a key challenge in open-ended discovery.

title: How many switches does two-Hamiltonian universality require?
abstract: Any pair of sufficiently generic Hamiltonians on $\mathbb{C}^d$ generates the full unitary group, i.e., any $W\in U(d)$ can be synthesized to arbitrary precision by alternating between the two evolutions for suitably chosen durations. For any given pair of Hamiltonians, the minimal number of switches required to cover the entire group is at least $d$ and unbounded in general. Despite this, we show that it scales linearly in $d$ in expectation. Assuming that the two spectra are sufficiently generic, we derive constructive upper bounds on the minimal switching number as a function of the change-of-basis matrix between the two eigenbases. In particular, if this matrix has a column whose entries all have equal moduli, as for a complex Hadamard matrix, then $9d$ switches suffice to reach every unitary. To obtain these results, we construct a short exact representation of any unitary as a product of unitaries that are alternately diagonal in two given bases. All bounds are extended to non-generic spectra and bounded evolution times.

title: Pushback in a Haystack: Language Models Respond to Factual Errors Ambiguously and Ineffectively
abstract: The sycophancy of language models, or their failure to push back against faulty user input, is now widely studied. However, if LMs do push back, is sycophancy solved? We show that LMs vary in how they present pushback, and thus vary in how effectively they correct user beliefs. We introduce a phrase-level, human-validated response labeling framework to uncover fine-grained insights into how LMs push against and/or affirm false inputs. We develop and apply our framework on model responses in five languages: English, German, Chinese, Hindi, and Yoruba. We find that when models do push back against users' false assertions, they tend to use indirect phrasing and mix in affirmation, with more indirectness in Hindi and Yoruba than in other languages considered. In a large-scale human study (n = 300), we find that the pushback ambiguity we identified may fail to correct and prevent users' factual misconceptions.

title: Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Models for Consistent Future Frame Prediction
abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Multilingual Abstractive Summarization: A Comprehensive Study of English and Bengali
abstract: Abstractive summarization remains challenging across languages, where linguistic quality and factual consistency may diverge, particularly in low-resource settings. We present a standardized zero-shot benchmark of eight closed-source and open-weight LLMs on size-matched English and Bengali XL-Sum test sets. Our evaluation combines lexical and semantic metrics with reference-free factuality verification and multidimensional LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, providing a comprehensive analysis of both surface-level quality and factual reliability in multilingual summarization. Results reveal substantial cross-lingual variation: GPT-5.6 Luna leads several English lexical metrics but does not maintain the same advantage in Bengali, where LLaMA 3.3 70B achieves the highest ROUGE and BLEU scores. Gemini 2.5 Flash obtains the highest observed Bengali factuality score. Furthermore, evaluation methods produce different model rankings, highlighting the limitations of relying on a single metric for multilingual summarization assessment. These findings demonstrate that strong English summarization performance does not necessarily transfer to Bengali and emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation frameworks for low-resource languages.

title: Dissociating Answerability from Extraction in LLM Question Answering over Radiology Reports
abstract: Answering questions from radiology reports involves two decisions: whether the report contains an answer and which span gives it. A false answer presents an unsupported claim as fact; an over-abstention hides what the report says. Yet RadQA results are reported as a single F1 that merges both. We propose an evaluation method that separates them, reporting false-answer and over-abstention rates beside F1 and splitting F1 changes into extraction and answerability terms. We apply it to 13 LLMs on the RadQA test set, zero-shot and with three cumulative demonstration sets, the last adding an unanswerable example. Models with similar F1 differed more than twofold in false-answer rate. The unanswerable example changed when models answered, not how well they extracted: 12 of 13 models abstained more often, and three-quarters of the answers they withdrew had F1 $\geq$ 0.5. Within models, false answers showed no clear association with extraction quality, but acting on the decision itself helped: keeping an answer only when enough other models also answered lowered the zero-shot false-answer rate by 4 points without a detectable F1 change. Because the two decisions can change independently, we suggest radiology QA evaluations report them separately, not through F1 alone.

title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.

title: Connecting the Dots: Enduring Performance Gaps in ASR Systems Between Standard and Minority English Varieties
abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system evaluations have consistently revealed performance disparities along lines of race, gender, socioeconomic status, and language variety. While these disparities are well-documented, they are often (implicitly or explicitly) treated as issues that subsequent, larger, and more universal models will correct. We challenge this assumption of steady progress in reducing accent-related performance disparities, conducting a longitudinal evaluation of 16 prominent systems released between 2021-2025 across 8 datasets representing diverse English accent varieties. We find that the performance disparity between Mainstream US English (MUSE) and minority accents is stubborn, not reliably declining as a function of time. Specifically, while systems are reliably performant on MUSE, minority accents are subject to risks of large performance degradations between generations of systems, sometimes worsening by 65% absolute Word Error Rate. We argue that standard ASR benchmarks enact an implicit language policy privileging Mainstream US English varieties. As such, these performance disparities reflect systemic failures of language technology development infrastructure that disproportionately affect underrepresented speaker populations.

title: CÆNL: Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning with Objective-Aligned Representation Control
abstract: Active learning changes the representations used to acquire subsequent labels. We study this interaction through Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning (CÆNL), which separates acquisition, Dynamic Collapse Regularization (DCR), and its coefficient policy. DCR penalizes a normalized within-class to between-class scatter residual above a frozen reference, with a separate class-separation safeguard. Fixed, scheduled, deterministic-feedback, and learned-feedback policies apply this objective. The analysis establishes scatter invariances, conditional local descent, and coefficient bounds, and shows why clean geometry alone cannot guarantee input robustness. Six-seed classification comparisons are complemented by a 104-run study with separate control selection and ten-seed evaluations on each of two backbones. At 60% annotations on ImageNet-100, entropy acquisition with DCR and MACC-Lite reaches 73.420 +/- 0.512% accuracy on ResNet-50 and 73.086 +/- 0.397% on ResNet-18 (mean +/- seed SD), exceeding entropy alone by 1.742 and 1.834 percentage points. Both gains survive Holm correction under paired-t and exact sign-flip tests, with unchanged feedback settings across backbones. Independently tuned constants attain slightly higher mean accuracy; the paired comparisons establish neither adaptive superiority nor equivalence. Separate six-seed spectral studies yield a small fixed-regularization C4 loss reduction, worse CIFAR-10 diffusion FID, and inconclusive AudioCaps captioning effects. Earlier classification studies find near-zero AutoAttack accuracy at L-infinity radius 8/255 and no added benefit from learned control. The results support the evaluated combined classification treatment and identify the task dependence of geometry-informed regularization.

title: Artifact for the paper ALIEN: an Automatic Lean Verification Framework for UFO Ontological Models
abstract: Reproducibility package for “ALIEN: an Automatic Lean Verification Framework for UFO Ontological Models”. ALIEN checks finite UFO models declared in a domain-specific language, produces reusable Lean certificates, and presents diagnostics for failed checks. The package includes source code, proofs, examples, regression tests, prebuilt Docker images for Linux ARM64 and AMD64, and the reference measurements used in the paper. Docker commands reproduce the evaluation tables from supplied measurements or run new experiments and generate a PDF of the results. Docker is the only required host software for this workflow, an optional VS Code walkthrough supports interactive inspection. Start with README.md and download the image matching your architecture. Immutable source: https://github.com/smnicoletti/lean-ufo/tree/alien-v1.0.0

title: RIDI Qwen3 scale curve: amendment A1 execution and analysis results (Supplementary Data 5)
abstract: Supplementary Data 5 for the RIDI study, “Identical evaluation scores conceal which questions language models answer correctly”. This dataset contains the completed RIDI-RAG-QWEN3-SCALE-CURVE-v1 amendment-A1 execution and analysis package: six Qwen3 model sizes across four benchmarks on a common panel of 800 questions, comprising 24 model-by-benchmark units. It includes selected per-question generation records, locked code, amendment A1, deviation 001, retained failed and interrupted attempts, combined analysis outputs, independent verification and source-archive SHA-256 manifests. Registration: https://osf.io/whjbs/Code repository: https://github.com/adeebnoor/ridiRelated source-data deposit: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22974727 The preregistered H1 and H2 criteria were met. The registered overall slope was positive, but the curve was non-monotonic, peaking at 8B; these results must not be described as a monotonic decrease with model size. The package uses the new scale-curve execution floor at 8B rather than the earlier primary-experiment floor. Original pre-A1 32B HotpotQA outputs are retained for comparison only and are not pooled into A1. Archival limitations are preserved: incomplete attempts remain incomplete; the five-size historical analysis file was not recovered and the explicitly labelled reconstruction is not represented as that original file. No human-annotation results are included. This deposit supplies data and analysis materials, not a journal submission or a new preregistration. Third-party materials remain subject to their original terms. Archive SHA-256: 0efd545c111ad161bd5669cc120e5457b1024ea258d7e3c59a7fc04ab708e0f2.

title: The Rectification Train: Recovering Meaning from Everyday Typing Errors Without Altering the Record
abstract: People type faster than they type accurately, and a growing share of the record, from chat logs and working sessions with AI systems to field notes and first drafts, is captured exactly as typed. Uncorrected text is often unreadable to search: the words are there, but no query can find them. This paper describes the rectification train, a staged method for recovering the meaning of damaged typed text while preserving the original exactly. It sets out why typing errors take the shapes they do, drawing on four decades of research on skilled typing as motor control; presents an eight-class taxonomy of typing anomalies, six classes from that research and two named here, including the Perimeter Key Co-activation Destruction Event (PKCDE); describes the six processing stages and the rules that govern them; records how the method was developed between 27 and 30 May 2026; and reports a computed test on thirty-one turns of everyday, uncorrected typing. In that record, search returned at least one hit for 8 of 15 fixed questions from the raw text and for 15 of 15 after rectification: a 1.9× improvement by question and 2.5× by turn. The method is a technique of Latent Value Query and runs on Generative Temporal Referencing. This paper discloses the concept, taxonomy, stages, and results; it withholds the implementation. It has not been peer reviewed.

title: An imitation enhanced actor–critic approach for maze navigation
abstract: Aims: This paper proposes a new method that integrates Imitation Learning (IL) into the Actor–Critic (AC) algorithm and evaluates its effect on the learning speed of agents in both obstacle and obstacle–free mazes. Methods: The paper presents a new method that combines AC with a model of simply imitating observed behaviour, without direct internal access or inter–agent experience sharing. The proposed Imitation Enhanced Actor–Critic (IEAC) learning approach is evaluated through simulations on a maze pathfinding problem. Results: Simulation results indicated that the proposed learning method significantly accelerated learning in terms of convergence speed and achieved higher stability compared to the standard Actor–Critic approach. In particular, agents using the imitation enhanced model reached optimal paths in fewer steps, in both mazes. Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that integrating imitation learning into the actor–critic framework enhances convergence and stability, particularly in complex environments with obstacles. The proposed IEAC approach has potential applicability in autonomous navigation and robotic systems requiring efficient learning from observation.

title: A comparative review of machine learning models and deep learning architectures for pregnancy progression prediction
abstract: Monitoring the course of pregnancy is of paramount importance, enabling the identification of negative outcomes and clinically significant changes. Although parity status may contribute to information needs, status as first-time mothers is not considered as a causal determinant. This paper presents a structured scoping review comparing conventional and deep learning approaches to pregnancy-related prediction tasks. The reviewed machine learning models include logistic regression; random forest; Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost); Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their gated variants, long short-term memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs); Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs); transformers; and hybrid architectures. The analysis employs six dimensions: performance; ability to encode temporal data; model interpretability; data requirements for training; computational costs; and clinical relevance. As primary studies report outcome-specific performance results, the findings are presented across outcome domains rather than aggregated rankings of model architectures. In a study on predicting preterm-birth outcomes, a transformer achieved a test-set Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) of 0.792, compared to 0.78 for logistic regression, 0.751 for random forest, and 0.717 for a Support Vector Machine (SVM). In predicting preeclampsia, a CNN achieved an AUC of 0.85 on holdout validation and 0.81 on an external test set, with an AUC of 0.98 for early-onset preeclampsia. CTGFusionNet, which employs a hybrid architecture of convolutional, recurrent, and attention layers applied to Cardiotocography (CTG) and clinical records, reported 97.85% accuracy for the task of fetal-distress classification. The findings highlight the complementary strengths and weaknesses of conventional and deep learning models for the analyzed tasks. The choice of an architecture should be informed by the target outcome, data type, volume, and quality, calibration and validation strategies, requirements for interpretability and fairness, and computational costs rather than a singular emphasis on performance.

title: AI Literacy for Leaders
abstract: This chapter builds AI literacy for leaders who have no technical background and no need to acquire one. The aim is judgment, not coding. It lays out a working map of the main technologies, from machine learning and deep learning through natural language processing, generative AI, computer vision, and robotics and explains each in language a board member could follow. It defines the few concepts that actually come up in the room: namely, training data, model architecture, and algorithmic bias. It offers a maturity model for gauging how ready an organization really is. And it closes by taking apart five stubborn myths about what AI can and cannot do.

title: Towards multi-QPU quantum systems: Circuit mapping for high execution fidelity and low communication overhead
abstract: Abstract Multi-quantum processing unit (multi-QPU) architectures have emerged as a promising route for scaling up quantum computing. However, quantum circuit execution across QPUs introduces remote operations, which have lower fidelity than local operations and require additional communication resources. Circuit mapping, which determines where quantum information and operations are placed, critically affects the number of required remote operations and, consequently, the reliability and efficiency of distributed execution. Here, we introduce NAVI, a communication- and noise-aware circuit mapping framework for multi-QPU systems. NAVI addresses three mapping decisions in a staged compiler workflow: how to partition qubits according to evolving interaction patterns, which communication mode should be used for remote operations, and which physical QPUs should host the resulting qubit partitions under heterogeneous noise. Across a diverse set of benchmark circuits, NAVI reduces cumulative execution error by 40% to 55% and communication resource consumption by 60% to 72% on average compared with existing methods.

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

title: Legal-R1: Agentic Retrieval for Evidence-Based Legal Reasoning
abstract: Legal question answering requires answers that are not only plausible, but also grounded in legally valid and citable evidence. Standard retrieval-augmented generation often relies on one-shot semantic matching, which is insufficient when legal evidence must be selected according to authority, applicability, and diversity across heterogeneous sources. We introduce Legal-R1, an agentic retrieval framework for evidence-based legal reasoning. Legal-R1 decomposes legal reasoning into a multi-agent workflow, where a Lawyer agent learns when to retrieve, which legal source to query, what evidence to seek, and when the collected evidence is sufficient. A Legal Assistant agent retrieves from normative legal sources and precedent cases with authority-aware and diversity-aware selection, while a Judge agent generates the final answer from the complete evidence trajectory. We post-train only the Lawyer agent with masked supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-aware reinforcement learning. Experiments on multiple Chinese legal benchmarks show that Legal-R1 improves over general-purpose, legal-specific, and retrieval-augmented baselines.

title: Bifocal: Training-Free Mixed Granularity Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal LLMs
abstract: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal

title: Toward Interpretable Quantum Generators for Financial Returns through Problem-Informed Circuit Design
abstract: When used as function approximators, quantum circuits often lack interpretability and face a fundamental trade-off between expressivity and trainability. We propose a problem-informed framework for financial return generation that uses relational structure and symmetry-inspired parameter sharing to guide the construction of quantum circuits with few trainable parameters and empirically testable operator roles. We evaluate three quantum generator architectures, referred to as ZZ, directed ZZ-CRX, and structured time evolution, within a hybrid Wasserstein quantum generative adversarial network trained to generate 16-step Bitcoin return windows. Across circuits with one to four layers and one to eight trainable coefficients, these generators recover meaningful marginal and temporal distributional features, while single-layer configurations remain competitive with deeper variants. Across matched depths, independently trained ZZ-CRX configurations exhibit a predominantly downward shift in median leverage relative to ZZ, consistent with the intended directional role of the controlled-rotation construction. The small number of coefficients also enables direct landscape analysis, revealing competing parameter preferences between marginal and temporal objectives and helping to explain the difficulty of finding parameter settings that perform well on both. These results provide an initial demonstration that structural assumptions can guide the design of compact quantum generators and link circuit architecture to observable statistical behaviour, motivating more systematic and parameter-efficient approaches to quantum circuit construction.

title: UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models
abstract: World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen. We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

title: A Few More Tokens Ahead: Reinforcing Parallelism in Diffusion LLMs
abstract: Parallel generation is widely regarded as an inherent advantage of diffusion large language models. Yet our fixed-quota evaluation of four representative models reveals severe degradation across mathematics and code, with all scores below 15% at 16 tokens per step. Token-level probes identify local predictive potential near the observed prefix, especially in mathematical text. We propose RePara, which reinforces short consecutive token blocks through group-relative policy optimization and reduces rollout and log-probability recomputation costs. On LLaDA and SDAR, \ours improves GSM8K and MATH-500 accuracy over JustGRPO under reduced denoising budgets, with a 1.96x training-step speedup in our LLaDA/MATH setup.

title: Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior
abstract: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. Real observations motivate these tests: on three benchmarks, simple predictors match or beat GPT-4.1. In two Who&When Pro systems, a classifier reading one step's reasoning finds 95-100% of faulty steps, motivating input restriction. In one of them, error injection leaves no reasoning after the faulty step; judges fine-tuned on its labels beat GPT-4.1 by 41 points. Adding task-related reasoning after that step moves this cue: fine-tuned judges lose 31-99 points, but zero-shot judges lose at most 9, motivating cue following. evidence.title: Auditing Failure Attribution: Label Predictability and Judge Behavior
evidence.abstract: Failure-attribution benchmarks ask an LLM judge which step or agent caused a failure. A high score should mean the judge checked the faulty step against the run (a cross-step check). However, spurious signals (surface cues) that predict the annotation can produce a high score. In this paper, we propose four tests to separate checking from cue use. Input restriction asks whether partial input predicts the annotation. Cue following checks whether moved cues change answers. Residual accuracy scores judges where cue-only predictors fail. Aggregation asks whether the failure mix or metric changes rankings. title: Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?
abstract: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

title: Zusammenfassung EDPB Guidelines on Anonymisation
abstract: Die Präsentation fasst die EDPB Guidelines 02/2026 on Anonymisation (Version 1, 7. Juli 2026, öffentliche Konsultation) aus der Perspektive von Forschungsdatenzentren zusammen und bewertet sie kritisch. Zentral ist das Konzept der relativen Anonymität. Die Frage, ob Daten anonym sind, muss demzufolge je Entität und Kontext geprüft werden. Vorgestellt werden der zugrundliegende rechtliche Maßstab, die beiden Prüfansätze (Simplified und Contextual Approach) sowie die drei Kriterien No Record Isolation, No Linkage und No Inference zur Bewertung der Anonymität. Um die Orientierung in der Guideline zu erleichtern, sind umfassende Verweise auf die entsprechenden Textstellen eingefügt. Abschließend werden Lücken der Guidelines aus Sicht der Forschungsdateninfrastruktur benannt, (z.B. die fehlende Berücksichtigung von Stichprobenunsicherheit, Mess- und Antwortfehlern, Zeit als Schutzfaktor sowie die fehlende Berücksichtigung der Forschungsfreiheit). Die Präsentation wurde in der AG Anonymisierung des Verbunds Forschungsdaten Bildung am 13. Oktober 2026 gehalten.

title: Windowed Hankel KEM: implementation, challenge instances and evidence for Windowed Hankel LWE
abstract: Reference and constant-time native implementations of Windowed Hankel KEM, challenge instances of the Windowed Hankel LWE problem, and the scripts and recorded outputs behind every figure of the accompanying paper, Windowed Hankel LWE: A Structured-LWE Problem for Cryptanalysis, with a Compact KEM. Windowed Hankel LWE is a structured variant of LWE whose public matrix is a Hankel matrix generated by one long pseudorandom sequence. Its hardness is an assumption: the known Middle-Product LWE reductions do not apply. The paper offers it as a problem for cryptanalysis; the KEM is research code and not for production use.

title: Türkçe ABSA’da Büyük Dil Modeli Tabanlı Otomatik Etiketleme: Başarılar ve Zorluklar
abstract: Bu araştırma, Türkçe restoran yorumlarında Hedefe Yönelik Duygu Analizi kapsamında, GPT-4o tabanlı otomatik etiketlemenin manuel etiketlemeye (SemEval) kıyasla etkinliğini incelemektedir. Araştırmada hedef terim çıkarımı (ATE), kategori ve duygu sınıflandırma alt görevleri; SVM, BiLSTM, MLP ve BERTurk modelleri kullanılarak SemEval, GPT-4o ve Birleştirilmiş veri düzenlerinde değerlendirilmiştir. Deneysel karşılaştırma, otomatik etiketlerin tek başına ve manuel veri ile birlikte kullanıldığında farklı görevlerde nasıl bir performans profili oluşturduğunu ortaya koymayı hedeflemektedir. Bulgulara göre, ATE görevinde SemEval üzerinde SVM yüksek geri çağırım ile öne çıkmıştır (Recall=0,8463; F1=0,7265). Duygu sınıflandırmasında en yüksek başarıya Birleştirilmiş düzende BERTurk ile ulaşılmıştır (F1=0,8336; doğruluk=0,9255); bu sonuç, daha geniş ve çeşitli veride bağlamsal temsillerin avantajını desteklemektedir. Kategori sınıflandırmasında ise en iyi sonuçlar Birleştirilmiş düzende SVM (F1=0,5183) ve BERTurk (F1=0,5108) tarafından üretilmiş; sınıf sayısının yüksek ve sınırların bulanık olduğu bu görevde performansın daha sınırlı kaldığı görülmüştür. Genel olarak sonuçlar, otomatik etiketlemenin özellikle duygu gibi daha net sınıf sınırlarına sahip görevlerde rekabetçi bir veri kaynağı sunduğunu; kategori gibi daha zor görevlerde ise etiket tutarlılığı, sınıf dengesizliği ve görev-model uyumunun belirleyici olduğunu göstermektedir. Bu çalışma, farklı model ailelerini birlikte karşılaştırarak otomatik etiketli verinin hangi koşullarda daha güvenilir biçimde kullanılabileceğine ilişkin pratik bir değerlendirme çerçevesi sunmaktadır.

title: Orchestration Frameworks for Agentic AI
abstract: This chapter focuses on orchestration frameworks for coordinating sophisticated agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems within single connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) systems, covering graph-based orchestration (LangGraph) and dialogue-based orchestration (AutoGen). The chapter examines theoretical foundations, practical implementations, and comparative analysis of these orchestration paradigms. LangGraph provides deterministic, verifiable workflows suitable for safety-critical applications, while AutoGen offers flexibility and adaptability for complex, dynamic scenarios. The chapter covers workflow design, state management, error handling, and integration patterns. It provides comprehensive comparison and selection guidance for choosing appropriate frameworks for specific CAV applications, emphasizing how orchestration mechanisms enable the practical implementation and deployment of agentic AI capabilities.

title: Jev-ToM: Evaluating Theory of Mind in Typed Decision Models
abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.

title: LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs
abstract: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.

title: Certifying Almost-Sure Reachability in Unknown MDPs
abstract: {\em Specification-Guided Reinforcement Learning (RL)} has largely concerned itself with \emph{learning} an optimal policy against a formal specification in an unknown {\em Markov Decision Process (MDP)}. We take up the dual question. Given a policy already in hand, can one \emph{verify} that it is correct against a formal specification in an unknown MDP, using sampling access alone? Such a question arises naturally in safety-critical systems. We investigate it for the {\em almost-sure reachability property}, whose correctness is witnessed by a {\em ranking supermartingale (RSM)} certificate. Our first finding is negative. In the absence of any further information about the MDP, one can neither learn such a certificate nor verify a candidate one with probabilistic guarantees. On the positive side, we show that, under a mild restriction, a known lower bound $p_{\min}$ on nonzero transition probabilities, a correct certificate \emph{can} be learned with PAC-style guarantees. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of learning and verifying certificates for almost-sure reachability in unknown MDPs from sampling access alone. Finally, our experiments show that the $p_{\min}$-based sufficient condition, while sound, is conservative: the learned certificate often remains valid on the true MDP even when the condition fails.

title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.

Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.

title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.
