title: 6G-HW10: 6G-Oriented Heterogeneous Waveform Dataset
abstract: 6G-HW10: 6G-Oriented Heterogeneous Waveform Dataset 6G-HW10 is a controlled synthetic dataset for heterogeneous waveform and modulation recognition from short complex-baseband observations. It combines traditional single-carrier modulation schemes, OFDM-based waveforms, OTFS-like and AFDM-like constructions, and a two-user downlink NOMA superposition under shared channel and RF-impairment parameter distributions. Key Features • Ten classes: BPSK, QPSK, 8PSK, QAM16, QAM64, CP-OFDM, DFT-s-OFDM, OTFS-like, AFDM-like and DL-NOMA-QPSK.• SNR range: −20 to +18 dB in 2 dB increments, with 1,000 observations per class/SNR combination.• Dataset size: 200,000 observations, each containing 256 complex samples represented as float32 I/Q with shape (2, 256).• Controlled simulation: shared settings for filtering, transmitter nonlinearity, time-varying multipath, carrier-frequency offset, phase noise, I/Q imbalance, amplitude variation, receive-window uncertainty and complex AWGN.• Fixed benchmark split: 160,000 training, 20,000 validation and 20,000 test observations, corresponding to 800/100/100 observations per class/SNR combination. Split seed: 2026. Data Format The dataset is supplied directly as a single HDF5 file, 6G-HW10.h5: X: I/Q observations, shape (200000, 2, 256), float32.Y: Integer class labels, shape (200000,), int16, values 0–9; these are not one-hot labels.Z: Nominal SNR in dB, shape (200000,), int16.class_names: The fixed class-label mapping.snr_values_db: The 20 nominal SNR levels.splits: Original zero-based training, validation and test indices.sample_metadata: 29 aligned generation-diagnostic arrays.metadata: Generation settings, field descriptions and source checksums. All signal values, labels, fixed split indices and per-sample metadata are preserved through lossless conversion from the frozen source dataset. README.txt explains the data structure, generation settings, scope and Python loading procedure. No ZIP extraction is required. Design Goals and Applications The dataset supports comparisons of heterogeneous signal classifiers, studies of representations for short I/Q observations, and evaluation across controlled SNR conditions. The fixed samples and split allow comparisons under the same benchmark conditions. Diagnostic metadata are not default inputs to the I/Q-only classification task. Research Context “6G-oriented” identifies the research motivation and selected waveform families. OTFS and AFDM have been investigated as candidate waveforms for next-generation wireless systems [1,2]. Here, OTFS-like and AFDM-like denote the implemented research constructions. The data are controlled synthetic observations, not standardized 6G air-interface transmissions or over-the-air measurements. No particular physical sampling rate, carrier frequency or mobility scenario is established. The two-file edition provides data and the fixed split, without the original generator or model-training code. References [1] M. Nie et al., “Towards Standardizing OTFS: A Candidate Waveform for Next-Generation Wireless Networks,” arXiv:2601.15048, 2026 (preprint). https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15048 [2] H. S. Rou et al., “Affine Frequency Division Multiplexing (AFDM) for 6G: Properties, Features, and Challenges,” IEEE Communications Standards Magazine, DOI: 10.1109/MCOMSTD.2025.3643183. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21704 Licence The dataset and README are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0). title: AI MATHEMATICAL DISCOVERY & INTERGENERATIONAL KNOWLEDGE EVOLUTION AT THE LIMIT A High-Density Research-Design Monograph on AI Reasoning, Formal Verification, and Mathematical Knowledge Succession STARLI | White Rainbow Civilization Mathematical Frontier Trilogy — Volume III Research-design edition | 13 October 2026 DESCRIPTION How can mathematical research remain inspectable, reproducible, corrigible, and useful to future generations when artificial intelligence participates in conjecture formation and proof discovery? This independently authored research-design monograph investigates this question through a three-component framework: AI Mathematical Reasoning × Formal Verification × Intergenerational Knowledge Evolution. Volume III completes a planned trilogy by shifting the focus from mathematical proof structures (Volume I) and cross-domain structural synthesis (Volume II) toward the institutions, formal artifacts, epistemic boundaries, and preservation methods needed for responsible AI-assisted mathematics. It proposes research protocols rather than claiming to establish new mathematical theorems. The monograph comprises 82 thematic chapters, each with one chapter-opening research relation and 12 individually paginated research units. Its six parts address: (I) research-oriented AI mathematical reasoning; (II) Lean, proof objects, and formal verification; (III) mathematician–AI collaboration and independent review; (IV) conjecture generation and counterexample search; (V) mathematical knowledge graphs, provenance, and proof archaeology; and (VI) long-term mathematical succession, model retirement, and open research governance. The final sections present 200 numbered Research Gates (G401–G600 in the trilogy-wide sequence) and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Research Gates are designed as executable entrances into unresolved work: each specifies an open question, a proposed test, an adversarial or stopping condition, and the evidence required for independent reassessment. The Answer Embryos are provisional research instruments that can be falsified, repaired, branched, or retired. A separate workbook indexes the chapters, research units, gates, candidate answers, and equation cards. The opening scientific preface contains 30 high-level physics derivation-route cards accompanied by conceptual three-dimensional geometric studies. Each of the 200 Research Gates and 33 Answer Embryos includes one distinct physics equation card, for a total of 233 equations. These retain their meaning within their original physical regimes; they are not presented as proofs of the book's claims about AI systems or mathematics. PRIMARY-SOURCE CONTEXT AND SCIENTIFIC BOUNDARIES The publicly available OpenAI Mathematics repository lists 719 manuscripts grouped into 372 families as of the public README consulted on 13 October 2026. These figures describe the reference catalogue and do not imply that this monograph has read or independently validated all underlying proofs. Repository content has varied in public versions; manuscript-specific claims should always be checked against their primary texts, available formalizations, citations, and version histories. Formal verification of an encoded theorem is not equivalent to proving that the encoded statement perfectly captures the original informal claim. Likewise, mathematical plausibility, numerical experiments, AI consensus, and persuasive exposition are not substitutes for deductive proof. The work is independent of OpenAI. It does not assert ownership of the original repository manuscripts, certify their correctness, or claim empirical results for the proposed research protocols. Its central contribution is an explicit research architecture in which negative findings, source corrections, independent reproduction, rights boundaries, and the freedom of successor investigators to challenge or replace earlier conclusions are treated as first-class scholarly artifacts. A mathematical civilization is not sustained merely by saving documents. It is sustained when future researchers can reconstruct the precise statement, revisit the evidence, inspect the dependencies, reject an invalid inference, and open a better question. title: Calibration, Conformal Uncertainty, and Fairness of Large Language Models for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction after ICU Admission: Evaluation on MIMIC-IV with External Validation on MIMIC-III
abstract: This is a preregistered retrospective, non-interventional prediction-model evaluation using publicly available de-identified ICU data (MIMIC-IV v3.1 and MIMIC-III v1.4). We do not train or fine-tune large language models (LLMs). The study evaluates three axes of LLM-based in-hospital mortality prediction: calibration, conformal uncertainty, and subgroup fairness, with external validation. Structured first-day (0–24 h) ICU features are converted into fixed clinical vignettes. A primary LLM (deepseek-v4.1-flash) outputs an integer probability (0–100) of in-hospital death. Baselines include XGBoost, logistic regression, and SOFA. No institutional PHI; CITI/PhysioNet training completed.

title: Nonlocal effects via local quantum Fisher information: characterizations and interpretations
abstract: Abstract We introduce a quantum Fisher information based measurement-induced nonlocality (QFI-MIN), which quantifies the maximal statistical distinguishability induced by locally invariant unitary dynamics. The proposed measure inherits desirable properties including positivity, local unitary invariance, monotonicity under local operations, and immunity to the local ancilla problem. Analytical expressions are obtained for pure states, arbitrary two-qubit states, and two-qubit X states, revealing a direct connection with entanglement for pure systems. The proposed measure admits direct operational interpretations in local channel discrimination and quantum parameter estimation. Specifically, QFI-MIN quantifies the maximal infinitesimal distinguishability and parameter-estimation sensitivity achievable through locally invariant unitary encodings. Its behavior under amplitude damping, depolarizing, and generalized amplitude damping channels demonstrates robustness against environmental noise. The proposed framework provides an operationally meaningful quantifier of quantum correlations, establishing a direct connection between nonlocality, quantum metrology, and quantum information processing.

title: Federated learning with update level noise perturbation and blockchain audit logging for privacy-preserving healthcare ECG classification
abstract: We propose FedChainDP, a federated learning framework that combines update-level noise perturbation with blockchain audit logging for privacy-preserving collaborative ECG classification across multiple healthcare institutions. Healthcare institutions face a fundamental tension: deep learning models require large, diverse training datasets to achieve high diagnostic accuracy, yet strict privacy regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR restrict the sharing of raw patient data across organizational boundaries. FedChainDP resolves this tension by enabling hospitals to collaboratively train a shared CNN model without exchanging raw electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. Each hospital trains locally on its private data and shares only noise-perturbed model updates, to which Gaussian noise is added once per federated round; these updates are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before transmission and logged on an immutable blockchain with Merkle-tree integrity protection and smart-contract policy checks on the reported noise parameters. Because this round-level noise schedule does not satisfy the assumptions of the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, the accountant output for the main configuration (ε_nom = 7.84 at δ = 10⁻⁵) is reported only as a nominal indicator, and no formal (ε, δ)-differential privacy guarantee is claimed. We evaluate FedChainDP on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia dataset partitioned across 5 hospitals using Dirichlet-based non-IID distributions. Our CNN model achieves 98.91% ± 0.14% accuracy under federated learning with update-level noise injection (σ_mult = 1.1), compared to 98.81% ± 0.31% for centralized training and 98.57% ± 0.17% for federated learning without noise-based privacy protection. These accuracies were obtained under a beat-level random split performed after duplication-based class balancing, so duplicated minority-class beats and beats from the same patients can occur in both training and test sets; they therefore reflect performance within this resampled benchmark and do not establish generalization to independent unseen beats or patients. A comprehensive privacy-utility analysis across noise multiplier settings (σ_multiplier ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 100}) demonstrates that classification accuracy remains above 98% across all evaluated noise levels. A black-box membership inference attack achieved 50.28% accuracy (near random guessing) against the noise-perturbed model; however, comparable near-chance accuracy was also obtained against the models trained without noise (49.16% centralized; 49.48% federated), so this result neither isolates a benefit of the noise mechanism nor substitutes for a formal privacy guarantee. A single-machine scalability simulation across 2 to 20 simulated hospitals produced accuracies of 98.90% (2 hospitals), 95.10% (5 hospitals), 93.80% (10 hospitals), and 97.20% (20 hospitals), respectively, while the simulated blockchain audit trail adds negligible overhead (0.059–0.091 s average mining time per block within the single-machine environment). FedChainDP incorporates technical safeguards relevant to healthcare privacy and accountability objectives across four dimensions: multi-technique privacy integration, blockchain-logged policy checks on reported noise parameters, smart contract access control, and empirical membership-inference evaluation.

title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.

title: EqC: Equilibrium Energy Control for Introspective Lifelong Robot Learning
abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC matches or improves control performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.
